subtitle: Greek-Speaking Administrative Elites & Gāndhārī Manuscript Culture in Taxila and Swat

events.title: Aramaic Inscription of Taxila (Sirkap, KAI 273)
events.summary: Imperial Aramaic as the Mauryan chancery language prior to Greek rule. Twice mentions Maran Priyadars ('our Lord Priyadarśi'). Demonstrates the Aramaic scribal milieu as the developmental foundation of the Kharoṣṭhī script (H1 Continuity).

events.title: Institutionalization of Bilingual Mint Chanceries
events.summary: Under Menander I and his successors, a standardized bilingual format is established: Greek legend (obverse) and Gāndhārī in Kharoṣṭhī (reverse). Attests an institutionalized scribal corps translating Greek administrative titles into Kharoṣṭhī (H2 Administration).

events.title: Reliquary Stupa of Meridarch Theodotos (CKI 32)
events.confidence: Very high (Original steatite reliquary in Lahore Museum)
events.summary: The Greek district title meridarkh (meridarches) appears in Kharoṣṭhī script on a steatite reliquary. Theodotos establishes relics of the Buddha Śākyamuni 'for the welfare of the many' (bahujana-hitaye). Direct link between Hellenistic administrative elite and Buddhist patronage (H3 Patronage).

events.title: Meridarch Copper Plate from Taxila (Shāhpur)
events.summary: Second attestation of a meridarch in Gandhāra, directly in the urban vicinity of Taxila: establishment of a stupa by a meridarch together with his wife in honor of his parents. Documents administrative officials as primary donors.

events.title: Urban Densification in Sirkap & Monument Jandial D
events.summary: Hippodamian street grid in Sirkap featuring immediate proximity of palace quarters, workshops, votive stupas, and monumental structures such as Jandial D along the northern main axis. Spatial interface of chancery and cult (H4 Urban Space).

events.title: Earliest Gāndhārī Birch Bark Manuscripts (British Library & Islamabad)
events.summary: Oldest surviving Buddhist manuscripts of South Asia. Their production falls stratigraphically and chronologically within the era of Indo-Greek and Indo-Scythian rule. Chancery-style cursive script and text layout indicate professional scribal practice.

events.title: Macedonian Calendar Months in Kharoṣṭhī Donations
events.summary: Eight Macedonian month names (Panemos, Gorpiaios, Apellaios, Xandikos, Daisios, Artemisios, etc.) are attested in sacred Kharoṣṭhī donations. The Hellenistic administrative calendar outlived Indo-Greek dynasties by more than two centuries.

events.title: Deposition of the Senior Scrolls (Kharoṣṭhī Pot Deposit)
events.summary: Closed collection of 24 birch bark scrolls preserved inside an inscribed clay pot dated to the reign of a Kushan ruler. Attests standardized canonical Gāndhārī scribal formulae and textual transmission under Kushan sovereignty.

events.title: Rabatak Inscription: Chancery Shift to Bactrian
events.summary: Emperor Kaniṣka I formally decrees the replacement of Greek as the administrative language by Bactrian ('Aryan language'), while retaining the Greek alphabet. Marks the chronological endpoint of the direct Greek chancery tradition.

events.title: Bajaur Scroll BC9r: Secular Statecraft (rājanīti) & Scholasticism on One Medium
events.summary: Andrea Schlosser (Nov. 2026) studies Bajaur fragment BC9r: the recto preserves 39 Āryā stanzas on kingship (rājanīti, attributed to Cakṣuka) in heavily Sanskritized Gāndhārī, while the verso carries a Buddhist scholastic treatise. Direct material evidence for the intersection of secular-administrative literature and monastic Kharoṣṭhī book culture.

events.title: Distinguishing the Kaniṣka Era (127 CE) from the Bactrian Document Era (223/227 CE)
events.summary: Studies by Salayev (Nov. 2026) and Bokiyev (Nov. 2026) incorporating the Almosi and Rabatak inscriptions distinguish the Kaniṣka era (127 CE) from the later Bactrian document era (223/224–227/228 CE) via internal synchronisms and tax receipts, sharpening the chronology of post-Greek chanceries.
